chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Al- from Al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Aban, [from Muhammad], from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:
I asked him about the borrowed item (ariyyah) which a person borrows, so it perishes or is stolen, so he said: 'If he was trustworthy (amin), then there is no liability (ghurm) upon him.'

He said, 'And I asked him about the one who manages the capital (istabdi'u) so it perishes or is stolen, is there a guarantee upon its owner?' So he said: 'There is no liability upon him after it turns out that the man was trustworthy.'

key_terms.يَسْتَبْضِعُ: Manages capital / Takes possession for trade

ai.seo_question: What is the liability for a borrowed item if it is stolen or destroyed?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the principle of 'amanah' (trustworthiness) in Islamic jurisprudence, distinguishing between simple custody and managed capital by exempting the 'amin' from compensation upon loss or theft. It reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on the borrower's moral status and lack of negligence as the primary criteria for liability, rather than strict liability for the item's fate. This ruling underscores the legal concept that a trustworthy custodian is not a guarantor unless explicitly agreed otherwise, aligning with broader principles of fairness in financial transactions.
